title: Explain Sliding Window — fixed-size vs variable-size window, expand right / shrink left.
shortTitle: Explain Sliding Window — Fixed-Size vs Variable-Size, Expand Right / Shrink Left

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The sliding window technique maintains a contiguous range over an array or string using two indexes, expanding the right edge to include new elements and contracting the left edge to drop old ones, so a running result is updated in O(n) instead of recomputing over every subrange. A fixed-size window keeps a constant width and slides one step at a time; a variable-size window grows and shrinks based on a condition.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh watches a rolling window of recent transactions. For a fixed window he always looks at exactly the last K transactions, dropping the oldest as a new one arrives. For a variable window he keeps extending as long as the running total stays within a limit and pulls the left edge in when it crosses the limit, so the window breathes in and out.

**One line to remember:** Expand right to add, shrink left to remove, and update the answer incrementally — turning repeated subrange scans into one linear pass.

sections.s2_technical:
A fixed-size window of width K first builds the window over the first K elements, computing an initial aggregate like a sum. Then it slides: for each new right index it adds the entering element and subtracts the leaving element at `index - K`, keeping the aggregate current in O(1) per step. For example, a rolling K-day sum: `sum += a[right]; if (right >= k) sum -= a[right - k];` and once `right >= k - 1` you record `sum`.

A variable-size window uses an outer loop that advances `right` to expand, and an inner `while` that advances `left` to shrink whenever a condition is violated or satisfied, depending on the problem. For a longest-valid problem you shrink while the window is invalid, then record the width `right - left + 1`. For a shortest-valid problem you shrink while the window is still valid, recording the minimum width each time it holds.

A code snippet for a variable window finding the longest span with sum at most a limit: `int l=0; long sum=0; int best=0; for (int r=0; r<n; r++) { sum += a[r]; while (sum > limit) { sum -= a[l]; l++; } best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1); }`. The left pointer only ever moves forward, so even with the nested while the total work is linear because each element enters once and leaves once.

The senior nuance is recognizing which variant a problem needs. Fixed-size applies when the window width is given. Variable-size applies when you optimize the width subject to a constraint, and the direction of the shrink condition flips between longest and shortest problems. Many string window problems also carry a frequency map or a matched-count to decide validity in O(1) per step. The amortized linear time is the whole reason the technique beats the O(n times K) or O(n squared) brute force.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India fraud engine watches Rajesh's spending and needs a rolling three-transaction total to flag bursts. This is exactly how a fixed-size sliding window works — add the newest, subtract the one leaving, keep the sum current.

Problem 2 — The same engine also needs the longest streak of recent transactions whose total stays within a daily safe limit, which can be any length. This is exactly how a variable-size window works — expand while safe, shrink the left edge when the total exceeds the limit.

The code shows a `SpendWindowAnalyzer` with a fixed-window `rollingSum` and a variable-window `longestWithinLimit`, demonstrated on Rajesh's transaction amounts.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: amounts [5, 1, 3, 8, 2, 4, 1], fixed width 3, variable limit 10.

Step 1: For the fixed window, the first three elements 5, 1, 3 sum to 9, recorded as the first rolling sum. As the right edge moves to 8, we add 8 and subtract the leaving 5, giving 1 plus 3 plus 8 equals 12.

Step 2: Sliding on, we add 2 and subtract 1, giving 3 plus 8 plus 2 equals 13; then add 4 subtract 3 giving 8 plus 2 plus 4 equals 14; then add 1 subtract 8 giving 2 plus 4 plus 1 equals 7. The rolling sums are 9, 12, 13, 14, 7.

Step 3: For the variable window with limit 10, right expands adding 5 then 1 then 3 keeping the sum at 9, within limit, so the window is width 3. Adding 8 makes 17, over the limit, so left shrinks: subtract 5 to get 12, still over, subtract 1 to get 11, still over, subtract 3 to get 8, now valid with window [8] width 1.

Step 4: Right adds 2 making 10, valid, width 2. Adds 4 making 14, over, so left shrinks subtracting 8 to get 6, valid, window [2,4] width 2. Adds 1 making 7, valid, window [2,4,1] width 3.

Step 5: The best width seen is 3, from the early [5,1,3] span and the later [2,4,1] span, so the method returns 3.

```
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Fixed window (k=3) rolling sums: [9, 12, 13, 14, 7]
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Longest streak within limit 10: 3
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The sliding window technique keeps a contiguous range over an array or string using two indexes, expanding the right edge to bring new elements in and contracting the left edge to drop old ones, while updating a running result incrementally. This turns problems that would otherwise recompute an aggregate over every subrange into a single linear pass. There are two flavors I distinguish clearly.

A fixed-size window has a width given by the problem. I build the initial window over the first K elements, then slide one step at a time by adding the entering element and subtracting the leaving element, which keeps the aggregate current in constant time per step. That is ideal for rolling sums and rolling averages.

A variable-size window grows and shrinks based on a condition. I advance the right edge in an outer loop to expand, and I advance the left edge in an inner loop to shrink. The direction of the shrink condition flips depending on the goal: for a longest-valid window I shrink while the window is invalid and then record the width, whereas for a shortest-valid window I shrink while the window is still valid and record the minimum. Even with the nested loop the work stays linear because the left pointer only moves forward, so each element enters and leaves the window exactly once.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used both in the fraud engine. A fixed three-transaction rolling sum flagged sudden spending bursts, and a variable window found the longest recent streak of transactions whose total stayed within a daily safe limit. Explaining the expand-right and shrink-left mechanics, the fixed-versus-variable distinction, and the amortized linear-time argument shows the interviewer I understand why the window technique is so much faster than the brute-force subrange scan.

keyPoints: Fixed window: max sum of K consecutive elements
Variable window: longest substring without repeating
Expand right, shrink left based on condition
